# Climate resilience adaptation and psychiatric emergency services utilization during extreme heat in Boston, MA: a difference-in-differences analysis

**Authors:** Flannery Black-Ingersoll; Mary D. Willis; Justin S. White; Stephanie T. Grady; Kaylin A. Vrkljan; Alison Duncan; Kate Burrows; Rachel Oblath; Amruta Nori-Sarma

**Affiliations:** aDepartment of Environmental Health, Boston University School of Public Health, 715 Albany St, Boston, MA 02118, USA | bDepartment of Epidemiology, Boston University School of Public Health, 715 Albany St, Boston, MA 02118, USA | cDepartment of Health Law, Policy, and Management, Boston University, School of Public Health, 715 Albany St, Boston, MA 02118, USA | dBoston University Chobanian & Avedisian School of Medicine, 72 E Concord St, Boston, MA 02118, USA | eDepartment of Psychiatry, Boston Medical Center, 850 Harrison Ave, Boston, MA 02118, USA | fDepartment of Public Health Sciences, University of Chicago, Goldblatt Pavilion, 5841 S Maryland Ave, Chicago, IL 60637, USA | gDepartment of Environmental Health, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, 655 Huntington Ave, Boston, MA 02115, USA

## Abstract

A growing body of literature shows that extreme heat events increase the risk of adverse mental health outcomes. However, the effectiveness of adaptation efforts has not been evaluated to date. This study investigates the implementation of two citywide interventions on extreme heat events in Boston, Massachusetts, focusing on psychiatric emergency services use.

Using a quasi-experimental study design with a difference-in-differences estimator, we investigate how interventions for excess heat and heat events may change daily psychiatric emergency services use: 1) heat advisory alerts and 2) a climate resilience adaptation plan. We flagged excess heat (maximum heat index ≥90 °F) and heat events (≥2 consecutive hours of heat index ≥100 °F). We linked heat exposures with daily total psychiatric emergency services encounters in a population of predominantly publicly insured and uninsured patients. We estimated incidence rate ratios (IRR) and 95 % confidence intervals (CI) in a Poisson regression, adjusting for temporal variation.

Among 110,656 encounters from 2005 to 2021, we did not find evidence of a difference in psychiatric emergency services use for heat events with and without advisories (IRR = 1.06, 95 % CI: 0.93, 1.19). Among 48,973 encounters from 2014 to 2019, we did not find evidence of a difference in psychiatric emergency services use for extreme heat events before compared to after the climate adaptation plan implementation (IRR = 1.03, 95 % CI: 0.97, 1.09).

Our findings did not show protective effects of two citywide interventions for excess heat and heat events on psychiatric services use.

## Background

The intensity, duration, and frequency of extreme heat is increasing due to climate change, threatening public health (Ebi et al., 2021b). A wide range of adverse physical health outcomes have been associated with extreme heat, and emerging evidence suggests that heat exposure is likewise linked to adverse mental health outcomes (Ebi et al., 2021a). Mental health outcomes of concern include anxiety and mood disorders, substance-use disorders, and self-harm. There are several pathways through which heat exposure may effect mental health outcomes. Extreme heat may disrupt sleep and physical activity, both of which effect mental health (Mullins & White, 2019). Sleep disruptions are linked to increases in mental stress and the exacerbation of underlying mental health disorders (Liu et al., 2021). Mental health behaviors may be impacted through physical distress and result in agitation, aggression, and increased substance-use (Cornali et al., 2004; Lickiewicz et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020). Additionally, some medications used to treat mental illnesses affect the body’s capacity to adapt to heat physiologically (referred to as thermoregulation capacity) (Lavigne et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2021; Nori-Sarma et al., 2022; Yoo et al., 2021). Given the growing body of evidence linking extreme heat exposure to adverse mental health outcomes, there is a need to understand existing and potential interventions that support mental health during extreme heat events.

Many cities are responding to climate change concerns by developing climate resilience adaptation plans, including Boston, Massachusetts (City of Boston, MA, 2016). Climate resilience plans have the potential to mitigate some of the public health hazards associated with extreme heat exposure; however, many heatwave early warning systems are explicitly developed to address physical health concerns from extreme heat (Lowe et al., 2011). As such, the literature evaluating the effectiveness of heat warning system has focused only on physical outcomes. Results are mixed: studies find reduced mortality due to heat warning systems (Benmarhnia et al., 2016; Boeckmann & Rohn, 2014; Heo et al., 2019), no change in mortality (Weinberger et al., 2018, 2021), and increases in morbidity (Thomson et al., 2023; Weinberger et al., 2021). This study is centered on the gap in the literature, wherein the existing literature on heat warning systems and morbidity and mortality is primarily focused on physical health endpoints and also describes mixed effects of the systems overall. To determine whether additional systems aimed at specific mental health endpoints need to be developed, we must first evaluate the effectiveness of these systems in the mental health context.

The difference-in-differences approach is a quasi-experimental study design that enables the estimation of causal effects of implemented policies. This method addresses unmeasured confounding by differencing out confounding factors that are time-invariant (Wing et al., 2018). Comparison groups in difference-in-differences models must be exchangeable (similar compositions between groups across the study period) and have parallel trends (parallel outcome trajectories if a policy or intervention is not implemented) (Wang et al., 2024; Wing et al., 2018). These assumptions support the conclusion that any differences in effect estimates observed between treatment and comparison groups can be attributed to the policy or intervention that was implemented (Wang et al., 2024).

In summary, the effectiveness of heatwave adaptation efforts has not been adequately evaluated in the context of mental health. As the body of evidence demonstrating associations between extreme heat and adverse mental health outcomes grows, it is necessary to evaluate the effectiveness of existing adaptation efforts. Establishing the effectiveness of existing efforts across a greater breadth of adverse health outcomes will provide policy-relevant evidence to guide further developments of more targeted adaptations addressing both physical and mental health endpoints. Using data on psychiatric emergency services utilization in Boston, Massachusetts, we conducted a quasi-experimental study to investigate the complex interplay of heat alerts, climate adaptation programs, and adverse mental health outcomes within a safety net hospital system. Our goal was to leverage the difference-in-differences causal inference method to identify the effectiveness of climate adaptations and heat alerts while controlling for potential unmeasured confounding (such as additional policy changes that may have occurred during the study period). This research assesses opportunities to improve health protection among Boston’s most vulnerable residents in a way that could be generalized to ongoing heat adaptation planning in other communities.

## Methods

### Study population

We used data on the all-cause psychiatric emergency services use from the Boston Emergency Services Team (BEST), a multi-channel psychiatric emergency services program managed by New England’s largest safety net hospital that serves low-income and under resourced patients and serves approximately 18,000 patients per year (Boston Medical Center, 2024; Oblath et al., 2023). Channels for care include emergency transport, walk-ins, and referrals, with evaluations conducted in emergency departments, urgent care, and mobile crisis centers.

This research has been approved by the Boston University Institutional Review Board (H-44251).

### Exposure assessment

#### Heat index

In the climate adaptation plan analysis, we compared days with maximum heat index ≥90 °F to days with maximum heat index <90 °F. This threshold was chosen to identify hot days based on the Boston heat advisory threshold (heat advisories are issued for Boston when the heat index is forecast to exceed 90 °F for 3 or more consecutive days) (City of Boston Emergency Management, 2024). We evaluated heat index using temperature and relative humidity data from the Boston Logan International Airport National Weather Station via the Global Historical Climatology Network at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) (Menne, Durre, Korzeniewski, et al., 2012; Menne, Durre, Vose, et al., 2012). This is the same weather station used to determine whether a heat alert should be issued for the Greater Boston area. We used the Rothfusz regression, following the National Weather Service’s method, to calculate the heat index (Rothfusz, 1990). The heat index is a commonly used heat exposure metric for estimating how hot it feels based on ambient temperature and relative humidity (Anderson et al., 2013).

#### Heat advisories

We filtered for ‘heat advisories’ from the weather alert archive on Iowa Environmental Mesonet (Iowa Environmental Mesonet, Iowa State University, 2025). This database provides daily information on National Weather Service Watch, Warning, and Advisories issued in US states (Iowa Environmental Mesonet, Iowa State University, 2025). To identify days with heat events that met the heat advisory definition for Massachusetts, we used hourly ambient temperature and relative humidity observations from the National Centers for Environmental Information at NOAA to calculate hourly heat index, flagging days with at least two consecutive hours of a heat index ≥100 °F as heat event days (Kantor et al., 2023). The heat warning system for the city is based on meteorological data collected at the National Weather Station in the East Boston neighborhood at Boston Logan International Airport. The state-level warnings are for a heat advisory (daytime heat index for at least two hours between 100 and 104 °F) or an excessive heat warning (daytime heat index greater than or equal to 105 °F for at least two hours) (Massachusetts Emergency Management Agency, n.d.). As noted previously, the city-level advisory warning has a lower threshold: three or more consecutive days with at least two hours of a heat index of 90 °F (City of Boston Emergency Management, 2024). In late 2016, Boston introduced a climate resilience adaptation plan with city-level efforts to issue heat alert warnings, updating thresholds and interventions (City of Boston, MA, 2016).

#### Climate resilience adaptation plan

Boston launched a climate resilience adaptation plan via a well-publicized report in December 2016 (City of Boston, MA, 2016). The report provides projections for the local climate, assesses neighborhood-level vulnerability to climate-change related environmental hazards, and outlines the city’s resilience initiatives (City of Boston, MA, 2016). Environmental hazards discussed include extreme heat, stormwater flooding, and coastal and riverine flooding with initiatives to prepare communities, protect shorelines, and adapt with resilient infrastructure and building solutions (City of Boston, MA, 2016). The city outlines strategies for both heat mitigation and adaptation: expanding green infrastructure (e.g. increasing urban tree canopy), retrofitting buildings (e.g. cool roofs), updating the existing heat emergency action plan (establish different thresholds for subgroups with differing vulnerabilities to heat, expand cooling center network). While these strategies established goals for approximate timelines of completion, the actual timing of when these strategies went into effect is unclear; however, in the two years immediately following the publication of the plan, it is likely that the heat warning system and cooling centers were implemented. This implementation did not require substantial infrastructural changes. A map of cooling centers developed in the summer of 2017 by the Metropolitan Area Planning Council also provides some evidence of implementation (Un, 2017). We evaluated exposure to the city of Boston’s climate resilience adaptation plan based on the year of the encounter with psychiatric emergency services (pre- or post-2017, corresponding with the system’s implementation).

### Outcome assessment

We used daily counts of all-cause psychiatric emergency services use from electronic health records. For this study, we extracted electronic health records for 267,157 encounters for 83,965 individuals from 2005 to 2021. Each record contained data on gender and race/ethnicity as denoted by clinicians based either on the patient or clinician’s reporting. We evaluated housing stability using geolocated shelter addresses.

### Statistical analysis

#### Quasi-experimental study design

We conducted two quasi-experimental studies with difference-in-differences estimator to evaluate: (1) the implementation of heat alerts and (2) the effectiveness of the climate resilience adaptation plan. For each quasi-experiment, we specifically examined the intervention’s influence on mental health outcomes among the study population. The difference-in-differences method controls for unmeasured confounding from external factors, such as co-occurring local, state, and federal policies that may influence the exposure–response relation (Benmarhnia et al., 2016; Willis et al., 2022; Wing et al., 2018). The categorization of days by exposure and intervention is illustrated in Tables S1 and S2.

#### Evaluation of difference-in-differences assumptions

We tested the key assumptions for a difference-in-differences estimator: compositional change and parallel trends. For both quasi-experiments, we checked for differences in sociodemographic characteristics in the comparison groups: for difference-in-differences (1), heat events on heat alert days vs heat events on non-heat alert days; for difference-in-differences (2), pre- vs. post-implementation populations. In difference-in-differences (1) we assessed the trend in psychiatric emergency services use in the days prior to heat events with alerts compare to those without alerts. In difference-in-differences (2), we assessed the trend in psychiatric emergency services use in the pre-implementation period for days with extreme heat compared to days without extreme heat.

#### Statistical analysis for heat alerts

We examined differences by alert (heat advisory/no heat advisory) and event occurrence (heat event/no heat event) for daily psychiatric emergency services use during summer months 2005–2021 (summer months are considered May-September in the Northeastern US; we considered May-September all years except September 2021, as 2021 records were only available for May-August). Heat events were operationalized as a day with at least two consecutive hours of a heat index at or exceeding 100 °F in accordance with the state-level heat alert threshold (Massachusetts Emergency Management Agency, n.d.). Heat alerts were classified based on the day on which the state-level heat alert was first issued (i.e. multi-day events were characterized by the presence or absence of an alert on the first day). We also examined this model by several strata, including pre- and post-implementation of climate resilience adaptation plan and sociodemographic variables (e.g., age, gender, race/ethnicity, housing status).

We look for differences in outcomes for heat events with heat alert warnings (true positive) as compared to heat events without heat alert warnings (false negative), heat warnings without heat events (false positive), and days without heat warnings or events (true negative) (Table S1). Examining counts of daily psychiatric emergency services use as the outcome, we construct the model in Eq. (1).

$$ (1) Y 1 = α + β f E H + β m H W + β f m E H ⋅ H W + ∈ $$

where HW indicates a heat warning (1) or no warning (0) and EH indicates an extreme heat event (at least two consecutive hours of a heat event at or exceeding 100 °F), α is the intercept and ∊ the idiosyncratic error term. We include all years of psychiatric emergency department data (2005–2021). To control for the impact of the climate resilience adaptation plan, which included efforts to disperse heat alerts to the greater Boston area, we also stratify the analysis by pre- and post-system implementation.

We used a Poisson regression to calculate the incidence rate ratio for the association between heat advisories, heat event days, and psychiatric emergency services use, adjusting for temporal patterns (holidays, year, day of week, week, and month).

#### Statistical analysis for climate adaptation program

We examined differences by extreme heat (yes/no) and policy implementation (pre/post) (Table S2). Extreme heat was operationalized as days with a maximum heat index at or exceeding 90 °F. Policy implementation was defined as before (2014–2016) and after 2017 (2017–2019), the year when Climate Ready Boston was supposed to be implemented. In this model, we looked at differences in psychiatric emergency department visit counts overall and stratified by sociodemographic variables (e.g., age, gender, race/ethnicity, housing status).

Examining counts of daily psychiatric emergency services use as the outcome, we constructed the model in Eq. (2).

$$ (2) Y 2 = α + β f E H + β m C A P + β f m E H ⋅ C A P + ∈ $$

where CAS indicates pre (0) or post (1) implementation of the climate adaptation program, EH indicates extreme heat (daily maximum heat index at or exceeding 90 °F), α is the intercept and ∊ the idiosyncratic error term. To examine changes occurring closer to the implementation of the plan, in difference-in-differences (1) we use a subset of years of available electronic health records: 2014–2019. We used a Poisson regression model to calculate the incidence rate ratio of the association between extreme heat events and the implemented climate resilience adaptation plan. We adjusted for temporal patterns (holidays, year, day of week, week, and month) (Supplemental Material S3).

#### Cause-specific analyses

In addition to the all-cause psychiatric emergency services use outcome, we ran cause-specific analyses for both the heat alerts and the climate adaptation program analyses. The cause-specific analyses categorize mental health diagnoses into disorders, as previously done in analyses conducted in this population (Oblath et al., 2023). These are: stress and adjustment disorders, mood disorders, anxiety disorders, non-mood psychotic disorders, childhood onset disorders, substance use disorders, or other psychiatric disorders. The study data do not differentiate primary and secondary diagnoses; therefore, we conducted further sensitivity testing to examine single diagnosis cause-specific analyses.

#### Sensitivity analyses

We also ran a sensitivity analysis looking at a subset of unique daily visits, where only the first visit within a given day is counted towards the total daily visits for both statistical analyses. We conducted this sensitivity analysis for both the heat advisory and climate resilience adaptation plan analyses. We also assessed whether the timing of the climate adaptation plan may have affected the assessment of the true effect due to any delays in implementation of the cooling center and threshold changes by shifting the intervention year to 2018 (omitting 2017 under the assumption that implementation may have been underway but not complete until 2018).

## Results

### Descriptive Statistics

#### Heat advisories and psychiatric emergency services use during heat events

In the first difference-in-differences study (Table 1), we looked at summer month heat advisory warnings from 2005 to 2021. There were 110,656 psychiatric emergency services use, with a predominantly nonLatino White (38.6 %) and non-Latino Black (30.7 %) study population. Over the study period, there were 19 days (905 psychiatric emergency services use) with advisories and events and 2,440 days (104,586 visits) with no advisory and no event (Table S3). The most common psychiatric diagnoses in this study were mood disorders (50.1 %) and substance use disorders (32.6 %) (Table S4). These two subsets represent “true positive” and “true negative” heat advisory warnings. The exposure data demonstrate inaccuracies in heat advisory warnings: 10 heat event days (388 visits) had no advisory, and 97 days had an advisory but no event (4,777 visits) (Tables 1 and 2). We did not find evidence of a violation of the parallel-trends assumption, as assessed via the event study plots provided in the Supplemental Material S2. We found that heat alerts occurred more frequently for event days with higher mean heat indices (Fig. S1).

#### Climate adaptation program implementation and psychiatric emergency services use on hot days

In the months of May through September from 2014 to 2019, there were 48,973 psychiatric emergency services use (Table 4). The majority of patients were cis-gender male (55.7 %), ages 18–44 (50.9 %), with 39.9 % non-Latino White, 31.2 % non-Latino Black, and 17.3 % Latino. A sizeable portion of the study population was experiencing homelessness at the time of their encounter (25.7 %), likely an underestimate as those experiencing homelessness without a geolocation (temporary housing such as a shelter) were not included in the final set of cleaned and geocoded electronic health records (Fig. S2). The most common psychiatric diagnoses in this study were mood disorders (46.3 %) and substance use disorders (30.4 %) (Table S4). In the pre-implementation period from 2014 to 2016, there were 420 days with a maximum daily heat index below 90° F and 39 days with a maximum daily heat index at or exceeding 90° F. In the post-implementation period from 2017 to 2019, there were 400 days with a maximum daily heat index below 90° F and 54 days with a maximum daily heat index at or exceeding 90° F. We did not find evidence of a violation of the parallel-trends assumption, as assessed via the event study plots provided in the Supplemental Material S2.

### Main statistical models

#### Heat advisories and psychiatric emergency services use during heat events

We found no evidence an association between heat events with advisories changing psychiatric emergency services use among patients compared to heat events occurring without advisories (IRR = 1.06, 95 % CI: 0.93, 1.19). Stratifying by pre- and post- implementation of the climate resilience adaptation system, similarly null effects pre-period (IRR = 0.96, 95 % CI: 0.78, 1.18) as well as post-period (IRR = 1.01, 95 % CI: 0.86, 1.18). The IRRs for overall and sociodemographic stratifications of the difference-in-differences are provided in Table 3. We found increased psychiatric emergency services use among the Latino population subgroup (IRR = 1.68, 95 % CI: 1.22, 2.35); other stratified estimates did not show evidence of heat event days with heat advisories changing psychiatric emergency services use compared to heat events on days without advisories.

#### Climate adaptation program implementation and psychiatric emergency services use on hot days

We did not find an association between extreme heat events occurring after the implementation of the climate adaptation program and psychiatric emergency services use when comparing with events occurring prior to implementation (IRR = 1.03, 95 % CI: 0.97, 1.09). The IRRs for overall and sociodemographic stratifications of the difference-in-differences are provided in Table 5. Similar IRRs to the overall estimate were found for unhoused patients (IRR = 0.98, 95 % CI: 0.87, 1.11) and unhoused patients (IRR = 1.04, 95 % CI: 0.97, 1.12). We also note that the event study plots for this analysis may provide insight into potential delayed onset associations; however, we do not see consistent differences in the association in the years following implementation, demonstrating no evidence of delayed onset (Fig. S8).

### Cause-specific analyses

In both the heat alerts and climate adaptation program analyses, cause-specific analyses yielded similar findings to the main models (Tables S4–S7, Figs. S15–S22). We found little evidence of a consistent association between heat events with advisories and psychiatric emergency services use in cause-specific diagnosis categories. Moreover, we do not see clear evidence of any association in cause-specific diagnosis categories in the climate adaptation program analysis.

### Sensitivity analyses

Removing recurring daily visits in both models led to similar results. In the model examining heat advisories and psychiatric emergency services use during heat events, the total number of visits decreased from 110,656 to 106,931 (Table S9) and the results were similar to the main model (IRR = 1.07, 95 % CI: 0.94, 1.21) (Table S10). In the model examining the climate resilience adaptation plan implementation and visits on hot days, removing recurring daily visits decreased the total number of visits from 48,973 to 46,804 (Table S11) and the results were similar to the main model (IRR = 0.97, 95 % CI: 0.9, 1.04) (Table S12).

Shifting the year of the climate resilience adaptation plan implementation to 2018 (and omitting 2017) to consider possible delayed implementation of proposed interventions yielded results similar to the main model (IRR = 0.99, 95 % CI: 0.93, 1.06) (Table S14).

## Discussion

Using a rigorous pair of quasi-experiments with difference-in-differences estimators, we did not find evidence that interventions aimed at reducing climate change impacts yielded any reductions in psychiatric emergency services use during hot days or heat events. However, the Latino population showed an increased use of psychiatric emergency services during heat event days with alerts, though the reason for this specific elevated risk is unclear. The subgroup finding for the Latino population may be attributable to weaker parallel trends prior to climate resilience adaptation plan implementation (Fig. S11). We did not find race/ethnicity-specific effect estimates in prior relevant studies (Ebi et al., 2004; Weinberger et al., 2021) nor did we find prior evidence of gender modifying the exposure-outcome relationship in the literature on heat alerts or heat alert systems (Heo et al., 2019). The totality of this evidence shows that neither intervention was effective at reducing psychiatric emergency services use during heat events. To our knowledge, this study is the first of its kind to examine whether heat warning systems and cooling centers reduce the burden of adverse mental health outcomes.

Limited research to date evaluates the effectiveness of heat alerts as public health interventions. Heat warning systems are primarily focused on providing the public with information on the breadth of evidence of adverse heat-related physical health outcomes (City of Boston Emergency Management, 2019; Nori-Sarma et al., 2022). Although our findings are largely null, previous studies yield mixed results with a range of physical health outcomes. Research on a similar system in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania examined heat wave warnings and excess mortality, showing a decrease in mortality by 2.6 lives for days with compared to days without warnings (Ebi et al., 2004). However, a casecrossover study of heat alerts in 20 U.S. cities found largely null results, with some cities showing a small increase mortality on heat alert days (Weinberger et al., 2018). A national-scale study of heat alerts and all-cause mortality among Medicare beneficiaries also found no evidence of reductions in mortality with the implementations of heat alerts (Weinberger et al., 2021). Although no studies to date have examined mental health outcomes, our null findings contribute to a body of literature with mixed findings, suggesting that heat alert systems may not provide the hypothesized health benefits in all contexts or for all populations.

While there is a research investigating the effectiveness of individual-level heat adaptations for physical health outcomes (e.g., air conditioners) (Boeckmann & Rohn, 2014), little work has evaluated the effectiveness local public health interventions for population health outcomes (e.g., cooling stations, hydration and water features, heat warnings with health advisories). Using a similar study design, an evaluation of a heat action plan in Montreal, Quebec found that the heat action plan was associated with decreases in daily mortality (2.5 deaths per day, 95 % CI: −0.34, 5.38) (Benmarhnia et al., 2016). The system in Montreal is comprised of a more comprehensive set of actions triggered in the event of a heat event: prevention strategies in health care facilities, extended public pool hours, daily visits or contact with home care patients, etc. (Benmarhnia et al., 2016). In contrast, we found no decrease in psychiatric emergency services use after the implementation of the climate resilience adaptation plan. We hypothesize that our findings could be attributed to several differences between these two studies. First, our study investigates a different health endpoint, psychiatric emergency services use. Heat alerts may increase awareness of the dangers of heat and the likelihood that individuals would utilize services. Second, our study population is a uniquely vulnerable subset of the Boston population, including a high prevalence of marginalized population groups (by race/ethnicity, income, and housing status). In contrast with our findings, the investigation of heterogeneity by vulnerable subgroups in the Montreal study revealed greater relative decreases in daily mortality post-intervention for neighborhoods with low socioeconomic status as compared to higher socioeconomic status neighborhoods (Benmarhnia et al., 2016). Our findings may reflect the challenge of overcoming a “double jeopardy” scenario, wherein the combination of socioeconomic and environmental exposures in this particularly vulnerable population subgroup is not effected by the climate resilience adaptation plan (Morello-Frosch & Shenassa, 2006). Additionally, in this study design, we are comparing the effects of heat warning systems within a population with a high baseline vulnerability to the health outcomes seen in patients using these psychiatric emergency services. It is therefore possible that any protective effects of this intervention are incremental in nature and therefore not visible in this comparison of this group to itself. This vulnerable population may also face barriers to accessing resources for coping with heat events, including the resources implemented during heat warnings and expanded following the climate resilience adaptation plan implementation, such as cooling centers, misting stations, and pools (Gronlund, 2014). Persons struggling with mental illness or housing instability may avoid youth and family cooling centers for fear that they would be out of place or unwelcome with families and children. Similarly, they may avoid using pools and splashpads if they don’t have children with them and may not have clothing to wear to these facilities or a place to change.

When interpreting the results of our study, there are some key limitations to keep in mind. First, the small sample size for the first analysis likely contributed to wider confidence intervals. Since we only had 10 days in total with events that did not have heat warnings, we were unable to further disaggregate alerts by events. Heat alerts for events occurring over consecutive days may also have different effects than those occurring for one-day. As the population adjusts to the heat with individual behavioral adaptations over the course of a several-days long heat event, psychiatric emergency services use may change. Third, if more intense heat events are more likely to receive heat alerts than less intense heat events, there may be circumstances wherein the population is not receiving the alert or the benefits of the climate adaptation plan because they are not triggered without a forecasted heat event. Fourth, the heat alerts are distributed from one weather station. We therefore assume that all patients are exposed to this same alert and the subsequent climate resilience adaptation interventions such as the opening of public cooling centers. This could be an inaccurate assumption if some persons in this low-income population (particularly those experiencing housing instability) do not have access to mobile devices. This would present a structural positivity violation wherein the subgroup of unhoused persons cannot receive the exposure to the alert if they do not have a mobile phone (Zhu et al., 2021). However, research on mobile phone prevalence among unhoused populations suggests that most persons have a mobile phone, suggesting that this is not a substantial limitation (Rhoades et al., 2017). Fifth, to assign heat index in both models, we used the same weather station that alerts the Greater Boston area to pending heatwaves, which leads to the assumption that heat index is consistent throughout the area and across all patients. Sixth, we were unable to evaluate the specific components of the heat warning system and climate adaptation resilience plan at large, as some proposed interventions may not have been fully implemented, which may explain the null effect estimates (Rickley, 2024). Details on the extent to which this plan was implemented are not published aside from evidence of the city-level heat alerts and cooling center implementation (Boston Public Health Commission, 2019). We implemented a sensitivity analysis to investigate whether delayed implementation may explain the lack of an effect observed, omitting 2017 and comparing pre (2014–2016) years to 2018 and 2019; however, we also did not observe an effect in this analysis. Finally, these findings may not be generalizable to the general population or populations of other socioeconomic backgrounds; however, investigating uniquely vulnerable populations remains essential to understanding potential gaps in adaptation efforts. In spite of these limitations, we were able to address a growing gap in research evaluating the effectiveness of a rapidly emerging array of urban climate resilience systems addressing increased frequency, duration, and intensity of extreme heat in the urban environment (Keith & Meerow, 2022; Meerow & Keith, 2022). Further research on mental health related outcomes in general population groups is also necessary given limited research to date on the effects of these interventions on these outcomes in any population groups.

Accountability studies, like what we presented here, are critical to assessing the extent to which these systems address climate change effects on health outcomes (Hystad et al., 2025; Rich, 2017; Willis et al., 2024). The development of these interventions requires considering a breadth of physical and mental health outcomes, vulnerabilities to adverse health outcomes, and exposure differences within population subgroups. A review of existing heat-health action plans finds that even plans recognizing heat and mental health associations do not incorporate specific actions to address mental health concerns during heat events (Stewart-Ruano et al., 2025). Interventions should consider that heat alerts alone are likely insufficient for populations without the resources to adapt in response to a heat emergency (Flocks et al., 2013; Toloo et al., 2013). The relevance of the Boston interventions in this population may not represent the effectiveness of the interventions for the general population and/or physical health outcomes.

## Conclusions

In this study, we did not find evidence of an association between either the climate resilience adaptation plan or the heat warning system for psychiatric emergency services use during heat events among a vulnerable population in Boston, Massachusetts. These findings suggest that the adaptation plan and the heat warning system were not necessarily effective at protecting mental health outcomes in this uniquely vulnerable population. Improved heat adaptation plans with measurable outcomes and services accompanying warning systems may be necessary to protect vulnerable populations.
